title: Which picture events get a sound, and which do not
when: Placing sound effects on a video's moments.
summary: Professional films sound a small set of picture events and leave the rest to the music. Most cuts have no sound of their own (about 85% in launch films). A press or contact gets one crisp sound on its frame; something appearing gets a soft pop at half its travel; a number locking on gets one tick on the final value; a big camera move gets a swish at its fastest point; the turn gets the music's drop or one impact.
do: Sound contacts, presses and lock-ins on their frame.
Put a swish only on camera-scale moves, about twice a film.
Let rolling counters and moving cursors be carried by the music, with one tick at the end.
avoid: A sound on every word or every element that appears.
checks: Fewer than one cut in five has its own sound effect.
source: earshot (Leonxlnx, MIT), pinned 4ac3d2a: real-sound sound-design rules, launch-video grammar; restated for narrated videos.

title: Hits land within a frame or two of their cause
when: Timing impacts, clicks, pops, swishes and risers.
summary: A sound that leads its picture by more than about 45 ms reads as 'sound first'; one that peaks more than about 75 ms late reads as late. Impacts align their attack on the contact frame, swishes their peak on the fastest frame, risers end on or just before the hit, beds start with their place.
do: Align impacts by their attack, swishes by their peak, risers by their end.
Compute cue frames from the picture, never from typed-in times.
avoid: Slow-attack samples aligned by their start, which land late.

title: Repeated actions draw from a pool of takes
when: The same kind of sound plays several times in a video (steps, pops, clicks, coins).
summary: One sample machine-gunned in a regular rhythm is a fast tell of cheap sound design. Use a pool of several takes of the same object, never the same take twice in a row, with a small level change (about 1-2 dB). Vary the take, not the pitch, for real objects.
do: Keep 3 or more takes per repeated sound kind when the library has them.
Cycle the takes and vary the level slightly.
avoid: The same take on every repetition.
Random pitch on typing or footsteps.
source: earshot (MIT), pinned 4ac3d2a: variation without randomness; restated.

title: The loudest moment sits on the turn, not on the ending
when: Shaping the music and mix across a whole video.
summary: A soundtrack with an arc has a quieter intro, a body, a peak on the main reveal or turn (usually between 30% and 60% of the runtime), and a resolved ending: the music stops on a bar or fades under the last line and leaves a soft tail. A flat wall of sound reads as stock.
do: Plan the music's peak on the video's turn or main reveal.
End on a resolved note with a tail into silence.
avoid: Music that dies before the last line lands.
source: earshot (MIT) levels and arc; motion-video-kit (MIT) audio rules; restated.

title: Choose music whose structure fits the film, and edit it on bar lines
when: Choosing and cutting music for a video.
summary: Pick a track whose shape matches the video (soft intro, a groove, a breakdown, a build into the turn, a resolve), at a steady tempo, instrumental. Cut it on its downbeats so splices continue the harmony, and dip it under dense speech instead of swapping tracks.
steps: Match the track's mood to the story's personality: calm stories get soft piano or strings, exact ones tight drums, bright ones marimba and plucks.
Ride the level: down under dense speech, up into the turn, down under the ending.
avoid: Meme sounds in a serious video.
source: earshot (MIT) music rules; motion-video-kit (MIT) back-timing a real track; restated.

title: Foley by material and scale, ambience by place
when: Sounding characters, objects and places in story shots.
summary: The same object always sounds like the same material. Size is told by pitch and closeness: small things higher and close, big things lower with a longer tail. Each place gets one ambience bed cut with the picture's cuts and dipped under key actions.
do: Keep one material sound per object across the video.
Pitch small things up and big things down.
Give each location one bed that changes when the place changes.
avoid: A different room sound on every effect.

title: The cheap tells of stock sound design
when: Checking a mix before it is approved.
summary: These make a soundtrack sound like random stock effects: synthetic beeps and noise sweeps, one sample machine-gunned, a whoosh on every cut, a boom on every title, sparkle sweeps for 'magic', reverb on tiny sounds, some presses heard and others silent, clicks at cuts, music chopped mid-note, an audible loop, and an ending louder than the peak.
checks: No whoosh on more than a few cuts.
No sample repeats with identical timing and level.
The ending is quieter than the peak.
Music splices are on beats and not audible.
source: earshot (MIT), pinned 4ac3d2a: the cheap tells; restated.

title: Every effect clear of the music in its own band, none harsh
when: Setting the level of each sound effect against the music and voice.
summary: An effect that adds nothing audible is wasted; one that spikes in the 2-6 kHz band hurts on phones. Each effect should sit about 3-6 dB over the music in its own frequency band, and bright pings and ticks stay soft.
do: Lift each effect a few dB over the bed in its own band.
Keep clicks and pings soft and centred.
avoid: Harsh high clicks spiking far above the music.
source: earshot (MIT) levels; motion-video-kit (MIT) quality bar effects-vs-music; restated.
